originalTitle: New York City's 'click to cancel' subscription rule takes effect, joining states with similar laws
summary: The Big Apple joins a growing number of jurisdictions adopting 'click to cancel' rules as the future of a federal standard remains unsettled.
content:
New York City has become the latest jurisdiction to crack down on hard-to-cancel subscriptions.

The city's new "click to cancel" rule, which took effect Thursday, requires businesses to make it easier for customers to end subscriptions that renew automatically. While New York state already requires a cancellation method be as easy as sign-up, this gives the city authority to enforce similar protections locally, and the city is providing a website portal for consumers to complain about violations.

"If a company can take your money with one click, you should be able to get your money back with one click," said Mayor Zohran Mamdani in a news release Thursday.

Read more CNBC personal finance coverage

New York is the first municipality to adopt a click-to-cancel rule, according to city officials. It joins a growing number of states that have enacted or strengthened laws governing automatic subscription renewals and cancellations as the possibility of a nationwide standard remains unsettled.

"Automatic renewals have been a pain point for consumers , and this is a popular topic with regulators, especially now given the increased focus on affordability, so I expect we'll continue to see more of these laws on the state level," said Gonzalo Mon, a partner with the law firm of Kelley Drye & Warren in Washington.

Complaints about 'negative option' subscriptions grow

Each year, U.S. adults spend an average of $1,080 on subscriptions, according to a survey by CNET , a media website focused on consumer technology. By generation, millennials spend the most annually, at an average of $1,215. The survey was conducted online in April 2025 by YouGov and involved 2,440 adults.

The survey found that consumers spend an average of $205 annually on subscriptions they no longer use.

In 2024, the FTC received an average of nearly 70 consumer complaints per day about hard-to-cancel subscriptions, up from 42 complaints per day in 2021, according to the agency .

Artificial intelligence may also be giving consumers a new way to deal with unwanted subscriptions. For example, Meta 's new AI agent, Muse , says it can cancel subscriptions on a user's behalf.

Meanwhile, more than half of states have rules that govern automatic renewals, Mon said.

"Although there are some variations, the laws generally address similar themes," he said.

The laws typically require up-front disclosure of key terms, consumer consent and confirmation, and an easy way to cancel, Mon said. Some also require renewal reminders.

What's going on at the federal level

The Federal Trade Commission finalized a national click-to-cancel rule in October 2024 under the Biden administration. It was quickly challenged in court by a range of business and trade groups, including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Federation of Independent Businesses.

About a week ahead of the rule taking effect in mid-July 2025, the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals vacated it on procedural grounds.

However, the FTC may make another attempt at a federal rule. In a March 13 notice this year, the agency sought public input on whether to update its decades-old Negative Options Rule, including whether to adopt provisions of the vacated click-to-cancel rule. Comments were due April 13.

Given the notice, "it's likely that the FTC will move forward, but we don't know how or when," Mon said.

In the meantime, the FTC has continued to pursue companies over their subscription practices using existing federal consumer-protection laws.

For example, the agency announced a $35 million settlement in May with Shutterstock over allegations of unfair and deceptive practices that included making subscriptions difficult to cancel.
chineseTitle: 纽约市的“点击取消”订阅规则生效，加入具有类似法律的州行列
chineseSummary: 由于联邦标准的未来仍不确定，纽约市加入了越来越多采用“点击取消”规则的司法管辖区行列。
chineseContent:
纽约市已成为打击难以取消订阅的最新司法管辖区。

该市新的“点击取消”规则于周四生效，要求企业让客户更容易终止自动续订的订阅。虽然纽约州已经要求取消方法与注册一样简单，但这使得该市当局可以在当地实施类似的保护措施，并且该市正在提供一个网站门户，供消费者投诉违规行为。

市长佐兰·马姆达尼 (Zohran Mamdani) 在周四的新闻发布会上表示：“如果一家公司可以一键拿走你的钱，那么你也应该能够一键拿回你的钱。”

阅读更多 CNBC 个人理财报道

据市政府官员称，纽约是第一个采用点击取消规则的城市。由于全国性标准的可能性仍悬而未决，越来越多的州已颁布或加强了自动续订和取消订阅的法律，该州也加入了这一行列。

华盛顿 Kelley Drye & Warren 律师事务所合伙人贡萨洛·蒙 (Gonzalo Mon) 表示：“自动续订一直是消费者的痛点，也是监管机构的热门话题，尤其是现在人们越来越关注可负担性，因此我预计我们将继续在州一级看到更多此类法律。”

关于“消极选项”订阅的投诉增加

根据专注于消费者技术的媒体网站 CNET 的一项调查，美国成年人平均每年在订阅上花费 1,080 美元。按世代划分，千禧一代每年花费最多，平均为 1,215 美元。该调查由 YouGov 于 2025 年 4 月在网上进行，涉及 2,440 名成年人。

调查发现，消费者每年平均花费 205 美元购买不再使用的订阅服务。

据该机构称，2024 年，FTC 平均每天收到近 70 起关于难以取消订阅的消费者投诉，高于 2021 年的每天 42 起投诉。

人工智能也可能为消费者提供一种处理不需要的订阅的新方法。例如，Meta 的新人工智能代理 Muse 表示，它可以代表用户取消订阅。

蒙说，与此同时，超过一半的州制定了管理自动续签的规则。

“尽管存在一些差异，但这些法律总体上涉及相似的主题，”他说。

蒙说，这些法律通常要求预先披露关键条款、消费者同意和确认，以及简单的取消方式。有些还需要续订提醒。

联邦层面发生了什么

在拜登政府的领导下，联邦贸易委员会于 2024 年 10 月敲定了全国性的点击取消规则。它很快在法庭上受到一系列商业和贸易团体的质疑，其中包括美国商会和全国独立企业联合会。

该规则于 2025 年 7 月中旬生效前大约一周，第八巡回上诉法院以程序为由撤销了该规则。

然而，联邦贸易委员会可能会再次尝试制定联邦规则。在今年 3 月 13 日的一份通知中，该机构就是否更新其已有数十年历史的否定选项规则征求公众意见，包括是否采用已腾空的点击取消规则的条款。评论截止日期为 4 月 13 日。

鉴于这一通知，“联邦贸易委员会很可能会向前推进，但我们不知道如何或何时，”蒙说。

与此同时，联邦贸易委员会继续利用现有的联邦消费者保护法对公司的订阅行为进行追究。

例如，该机构于 5 月份宣布与 Shutterstock 达成 3500 万美元的和解协议，指控其存在不公平和欺骗性行为，其中包括使订阅难以取消。
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于财经市场信号，适合用于观察利率、汇率、股债商品、金融机构和宏观政策变化。
